title: Indian American Muslims Celebrate Heritage and Patriotism at NYC India Day Parade
excerpt: The 44th annual India Day Parade in Manhattan drew over 150,000 people under the theme 'Harmony in Heritage,' with Muslim organizations marching alongside Hindu, Sikh, and Christian groups.
body:
• The 44th annual NYC India Day Parade took place on Madison Avenue on August 17, 2026, drawing over 150,000 people.
  • Indian American Muslim organizations participated in the celebration, marching alongside Hindu, Sikh, and Christian community groups.
  • The 2026 theme, "Harmony in Heritage," emphasized unity across India's diverse regions, religions, and communities.
  • The parade, organized by the Federation of Indian Associations, is the largest celebration of Indian independence held outside India.

Indian American Muslims joined tens of thousands of fellow diaspora members on Madison Avenue on Sunday for the 44th annual India Day Parade, celebrating their shared heritage and patriotism under the 2026 theme "Harmony in Heritage," according to News India Times.

The parade, organized by the Federation of Indian Associations (FIA), ran along Madison Avenue from East 38th Street to East 27th Street and drew an estimated 150,000 spectators, with millions more watching live broadcasts across 90 countries.

Unity Across Faiths

Muslim community organizations marched with floats and banners affirming their dual identity as Indian Americans, walking alongside Hindu, Sikh, Christian, Buddhist, and Jain groups in a display of India's religious pluralism.

The participation of Muslim groups carried added significance given the controversy that surrounded the 2024 parade, when some Muslim organizations withdrew over the inclusion of a Ram Mandir float. In contrast, the 2026 edition's "Harmony in Heritage" framing appeared designed to move past those divisions.

"We celebrate our unity in diversity, and we celebrate inclusiveness — that's our India."

— Avinash Gupta, President, Federation of Indian Associations

FIA president Avinash Gupta has consistently emphasized that the parade represents all Indians regardless of religious, linguistic, or regional background. The organization has invited floats from multiple faith communities in recent years, including Muslim, Sikh, and Christian groups.

A Growing Diaspora Flexes Its Influence

The India Day Parade has grown into one of New York City's marquee cultural events, rivaling St. Patrick's Day and the Puerto Rican Day Parade in size. An estimated 5.2 million people in the United States identified as Indian in 2023, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, with major concentrations in New Jersey, California, and Texas.

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill signed a proclamation ahead of the parade recognizing the 79th anniversary of India's independence and honoring "the courage, vision, and sacrifice of the countless individuals whose peaceful movement for freedom inspired generations around the world."

The parade featured dozens of floats, marching bands, Bollywood celebrities, cultural performances, and a food festival on East 26th Street — all reflecting India's regional and cultural diversity.

Heritage as Common Ground

For Indian American Muslims, the parade offered an opportunity to assert their place within the broader diaspora narrative. Muslims have deep roots in India's history, contributing to its architecture, cuisine, music, and political life. The Mughal-era monuments, Sufi musical traditions, and culinary staples like biryani and kebabs are shared cultural touchstones across religious lines.

Community leaders said the 2026 parade demonstrated that heritage and patriotism are not the preserve of any single religious group — a message they hoped would resonate in both the United States and India.

What the Parade Means for the Diaspora

The India Day Parade remains the largest annual gathering of the Indian diaspora outside India. For the 5.2 million-strong community in the United States, it serves as both a celebration of where they came from and a statement of their growing influence in American civic, economic, and cultural life.

The next major diaspora celebration on the calendar is Diwali, which New York City has recognized as an official school holiday since 2023.
